sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
A mass, a spring, and a viscous damper are linear elements: \(F=kx\), \(F=b\dot x\), and \(F=m\ddot x\). Newton's law on one mass gives a constant-coefficient equation, the same shape as any other second-order system. The natural frequency and the damping ratio are already defined. This skill is the map from the hardware numbers onto those two.

A shaft is the rotational copy. Inertia \(J\) plays the role of mass, a torsional spring plays the role of \(k\), and viscous friction plays the role of \(b\). Speed of a shaft with inertia and friction, and no spring, is first order, with time constant \(J/b\).

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[
m\ddot y+b\dot y+ky=u,\qquad \omega_n=\sqrt{k/m},\qquad \zeta=\frac{b}{2\sqrt{km}}
\]
\[
J\ddot\theta+\kappa\theta=\tau_{\mathrm{spring}}\ \text{gives}\ \omega_n=\sqrt{\kappa/J}.
\]
The signs matter. Spring and damper forces on the mass oppose displacement and velocity.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A 6 kg mass on a spring of 294 N/m with \(b=21\ \mathrm{N\,s/m}\) has \(\omega_n=\sqrt{294/6}=7\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) and \(\zeta=21/(2\sqrt{294\times 6})=0.25\). The same map on a shaft with \(J=1.8\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}\) and viscous friction \(0.75\ \mathrm{N\,m\,s}\) and no spring gives the first-order time constant \(1.8/0.75=2.4\ \mathrm{s}\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Using weight in place of mass. Drawing the damper force in the direction of the velocity, which is positive feedback. Mixing the rotational stiffness with the translational spring in one equation.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A settled step of this model is one of the records a later identification skill can fit. Cruise control uses the first-order rotational, or translational, drag model as its plant.
